title: Double Duty Strategies
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that in a job as demanding as teaching, the highest-leverage strategies are the ones that quietly accomplish several distinct objectives at once rather than requiring a teacher to run separate initiatives for each goal. He illustrates this with his MGC (moments of genuine connection) clipboard practice, showing how tracking brief individual interactions simultaneously builds student credibility, classroom belonging, mental models of each student, relational capital, and the teacher's own interpersonal depth, all from one habitual action. His second example, 'Woodenization,' the explicit, no-assumptions teaching of skills like note-taking and studying, is unpacked into a longer list of simultaneous payoffs: signaling that even small things are worth teaching, clarifying what good effort actually looks like, extending that clarity to every student rather than a remedial subset, and ultimately reducing the number of students at risk of failing. Stuart frames this as the basis of a deliberately 'minimalist' teaching philosophy, arguing a teacher can seek to be world-class at a small number of double- or quintuple-duty strategies and give themselves explicit permission to be mediocre at everything else teachers are nominally expected to excel at. The piece treats this permission to narrow focus, made possible by choosing genuinely multi-purpose strategies, as the practical secret behind his own classroom success.
points: Reframes teaching effectiveness as a strategy-selection problem rather than an effort problem, arguing the goal is finding the small number of practices that simultaneously serve multiple distinct objectives (credibility, belonging, relational capital) rather than running separate initiatives for each.

Unpacks a single habitual practice, the MGC clipboard for tracking brief individual student connections, into five simultaneous payoffs, making an abstract 'relationship-building' goal into an observable, trackable action.

Distinguishes 'Woodenization' from simple explicit instruction by tying it specifically to skills teachers typically assume students already have (note-taking, studying), arguing the act of teaching those assumed-skills explicitly signals value to the whole class, not just struggling students.

Names 'signaling belonging' as a direct effect of teaching effort strategies to all students rather than a remedial subset, connecting an instructional choice (who gets explicit effort instruction) directly to a classroom-culture outcome.

Builds an explicit permission structure - a 'minimalist approach' - arguing that mastering a few genuinely multi-purpose strategies justifies deliberately deprioritizing other expected teaching competencies, rather than treating comprehensive excellence as the only legitimate goal.
quotes: a great teaching strategy should accomplish not just one of your objectives as a teacher but rather many of them simultaneously. In a job as complex and demanding as teaching, we're after maximum bang-for-the-buck

When I'm working my MGC clipboard, I'm achieving several things at the same time: cultivating credibility with students by signaling that I care about them individually; cultivating belonging in the classroom by creating an environment in which every individual is valued, known, and respected; crafting mental models of each of my students, from which I can better teach them; building relational capital with every student in every class period; developing interpersonal depth inside of myself, this depth has greatly enriched my life outside the classroom.
if there's something I want my students to do well, it's up to me to clearly teach them how to do it
signaling value by teaching even small things that too many teachers just assume students know how to do
as students get clearer on what good effort looks like and begin to put it forth, I have fewer students at risk of failing

It really is true that I can simply seek to be world class at these few things, what I call the minimalist approach to The Will to Learn, and give myself permission to ignore lots of the rest of the things teachers are expected to be great at.
find the double-duty, or quintuple-duty, strategies and master the heck out of them
